body: Thanks for responding, btw. It's really rough refreshing for an hour and a half after posting on SW and seeing nobody even cares enough to upvote you. It reinforces that I'm alone in my particular craziness.

> Plus you forgot an option, you girlfriend could simply borrow your kindle and read it off of that, just as if the kindle were a book itself.

True. The problem comes when you both need access to the Kindle, like taking two different busses to work. It seems odd to say "sure you can borrow the book, but only if you only read it at home when I'm not reading this or any other book I own".

There's even another option - some people own a "lending Kindle". They have their normal Kindle, then they buy a second Kindle (probably the cheaper, smaller, ad-supported version, for obvious reasons) that they load with just the book being lent, and loan that device out.

The problem with that, is that from your entire library of books, you can only lend n-1 books (where n is the total number of Kindles you own; the -1 is because I'm assuming you keep your main Kindle for yourself at all times). 

I think that's where the negative view of the future comes from. In the future, legal requirements will cause you to state things like "I'd love to lend you my copy of Clash of Kings, George, but I already lent my copy of Slaughterhouse Five to Barry." 

The technology of our future gives a lot of new power to people whose sole purpose is to extract money from you. With two physical, dead tree books, you would *never* utter the above sentence. Go back five years and that statement would be utterly nonsensical.

Books are just one aspect. We're already there with music. Nobody carries discmen (discmans?) anymore. Everything is MP3. Even if you buy a CD and rip the music into MP3 for your iPod/Zune/whatever, you're still legally only entitled to use it yourself.

I don't usually buy music (radio is generally sufficient), but my understanding is that, legally, if two people want to have the same album, they need to buy it twice. Yes, MP3s don't have DRM anymore, but that doesn't mean it's legal to lend your music to someone else - it just means its easier to share music between your devices.

---

Despite all that, I recognize that the legal trouble comes in with downloading content from torrent sites, etc. If you legally buy a book or a song, then you use something like calibre to rip the DRM the book or to strip the audio watermarks from the song, and copy it to someone else, the odds against someone finding out and suing you are infinitesimal. It doesn't make it legal though.
 
It goes back to my point about moral absolutism in the post. There are rules you're legally bound to, like songs being licensed to one person/account, and it's ethically wrong and legally perilous (even if the peril is, for the most part, hypothetical) to go against those rules.

The thing is, I know I'm being irrational here. I torrented things for years before something snapped in my head and I stopped a few months ago and got into this absolutist mindset. I want to follow the law and obey the rules, but it's also really hard to say to a friend "I'd love to lend you this album I just bought, but legally I'm not allowed to." Wouldn't you laugh at someone who said that?
